chapter_theme: The chapter reports the period's rules for the meal (whom to feed first, direction, posture, order of tastes, rinsing the mouth), for the evening and for sleep, and for spitting and excretion, and it sets among them two ethics verses that bar even the sight and the thought of the gravest wrongs.
structure_note: Verses 21-26 the meal; 27-28 rinsing and the hands; 29-31 twilight, sleep and deference; 32-36 spitting, excretion, rinsing water and clothes; 37-38 ethical bars on sight and thought; 39-40 the hearth and kin at table.

21.reading: The verse says that those who never stray from conduct never eat without first serving food to five: guests, elders, the cow, caged creatures and children.
21.nuance: The list joins people and animals in one order of precedence at the meal: the guest stands first, and the cow and the caged creature (சிறை, read as birds or beasts kept in confinement; it could also mean captives) rank with elders and children as dependants of the house. The verse has no count word, so no items are given.

22.reading: The verse appears to say that the other directions too are good in their proper order for eating, and that those who approved eating along the line of the roof-ridge disapproved of laying the bed along it.
22.nuance: The verse follows 20, which fixes east for the meal, and allows the remaining directions in sequence. முகட்டு வழி is read as the line of the roof-ridge; it might instead name an upward or northern direction, and the contrast between food and bed turns on that word.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the directions for eating and for the bed

23.reading: The verse reports that the worthy do not eat lying down, standing, or in the open, do not eat to excess even when the food is choice, and do not eat on the bed, and it adds that one should not, breaking the rule, eat anything standing.
23.nuance: Excess (மிகவுண்ணார்) is set among rules of posture and place, so moderation is presented as part of a code of bodily decorum rather than as a matter of health. வெள்ளிடை is read as open ground; இறந்து on line 3 is read as transgressing the rule.

norm.note: a rule of the period on posture, place and amount at the meal

24.reading: The verse says that when people sit at a meal with those greater than themselves, they do not eat first, do not rise first, do not press close, and whatever they receive do not sit far to the right.
24.nuance: The greater ones (பெரியார்) are greater than oneself, by age or standing; the verse does not say by birth. மிக்குறார் is read as not crowding them and ஆற்றவலம் இரார் as not taking the right-hand seat, both doubtful.

norm.note: a rule of precedence of the period at a shared meal

25.reading: The verse sets the order of the meal: the sweet things first, the bitter things last, and the rest in between in the approved way.
25.nuance: The rule governs the food itself, its sequence by taste, where most of the meal rules govern the eater's body; the verse gives no reason, medical or ritual.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the order of tastes in a meal

26.reading: The verse seems to say that one does not seat the aged beside oneself at the meal, by rule takes a little of each thing eaten, and, without failing in affection or leaving ஆசாரம், puts away the vessel courteously.
26.nuance: Line 1 is doubtful: பக்கத்து வையார் may bar seating elders at one's side as equals, or may bar leaving them aside. Affection (அன்பு) and ஆசாரம் stand side by side as the two things not to lose, so the rule of the meal is tied to feeling as well as form.

norm.note: a rule of the period on seating, portions and clearing the vessel

27.reading: The verse describes the mouth-rinsing that the great have seen as the way: spitting out well so no எச்சில் is left and nothing drips, wiping well to the root, sipping three times and wiping, and touching the organs of the face with the fingers in the fitting manner.
27.nuance: This is a step-by-step procedure rather than a list of bars; வாய்பூசல் names the rite and the steps exist to clear எச்சில். அடியோடு is read as the root of the teeth or gums.

norm.note: a purification rule of the period: the manner of rinsing the mouth

28.reading: The verse reports that the worthy do not drink water with both hands, do not take from or give to their elders with one hand, and do not scratch their body with both hands.
28.nuance: The hands are counted in each rule: two hands are wrong for drinking and scratching, one hand is wrong for exchange with elders, so the same count is courtesy in one place and indecorum in another.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the use of the hands in drinking, giving and touching the body

29.reading: The verse says that at evening twilight people do not lie down, walk about, eat, grow angry or scorn the lamp, and that the way is to take the night meal and settle to rest.
29.nuance: Anger sits in a list of acts barred by the hour, so a moral fault is treated as untimely rather than wrong in itself. முன்னந்தி on line 2 is unclear: it may mean before the twilight, which would put the meal before dusk, or the twilight itself.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period for the evening twilight

30.reading: The verse says that on lying down one joins the hands and worships the deity, does not lay the head to the north or to a corner, and sleeps with the body covered by an upper cloth.
30.nuance: கோணம் is read as the intermediate directions; with வடக்கு it leaves only east, south and west for the head.

norm.note: a rule of the period on worship before sleep and the direction of the head

31.reading: The verse says that one does not pass between two gods or two பார்ப்பார், that when one sneezes and one's superiors bless one, one rises worshipping them, and that one goes along gladly with one's equals.
31.nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a caste term for brahmins, used here to mark persons who may not be walked between, alongside the gods. இருதேவர் பார்ப்பார் may be two gods and brahmins, or two brahmin 'gods'; either way brahmins are given the deference of sacred things. The verse ranks people three ways in three lines: brahmins, superiors (மிக்கார்) and equals (ஒப்பார்).

norm.note: a rule of the period giving brahmins, by birth-name, the deference due to gods

32.reading: The verse lists ten places where those with understanding neither spit nor void the two excretions: grass, green crops, cow-dung, the cremation ground, a path, sacred water, a temple, shade, a cow-pen and the place of the white offering.
32.nuance: The ten mix the sacred (temple, sacred water, the white offering), the useful (crops, shade, path) and the cow's things (dung, pen), so the bar protects both holiness and common use. வெண்பலி is read as the place of a white offering or of ash; it is doubtful.

items.claim: grass is a place where spitting and voiding are barred
green crops are a place where they are barred
cow-dung is a place where they are barred
the cremation ground is a place where they are barred
a path is a place where they are barred
sacred water is a place where they are barred
a temple is a place where they are barred
shade is a place where they are barred
a cow-pen is a place where they are barred
the place of the white offering is a place where they are barred

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: places barred for spitting and excretion

33.reading: The verse says that by day one does not face south and by night does not face north, and that by day one does not pour water into fire.
33.nuance: The verse does not name the act for which the directions are fixed; set between 32 and 34, both on spitting and excretion, it most likely concerns those acts. The water-and-fire rule is a separate bar tied to the same hour.

norm.note: a rule of the period on directions by day and night and on quenching fire

34.reading: The verse says that those who claim to live by the rule-book, having veiled the ten directions in their mind, spit and void only in a secluded place, and would not slight this even to gain the throne of Indra.
34.nuance: மனத்தான் மறைத்தபின் makes the screening an act of mind as well as of place. அந்தரத்து is read as a secluded spot; it could mean the open air. தந்திரத்து வாழ்துமென் பார் may carry irony toward those who only say they live by the text.

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period on where spitting and excretion are allowed

35.reading: The verse says that when rinsing from a vessel is not possible, people do not rinse the mouth standing in running water or in water lying on the path, nor without first marking off the place in their mind.
35.nuance: The conditional on line 4 makes the vessel the norm and natural water the fallback. நடைவரவு நீர் is read as flowing water and வழிநிலை நீர் as standing water on a road; both readings are tentative.

norm.note: a purification rule of the period on the water fit for rinsing the mouth

36.reading: The verse says that those who know their duty never pass between lamps, never spit on a wall, never take on themselves a soiled cloth worn below even in trouble, never go with their cloth blowing in the wind even if an army comes, and never shake out their cloth among many people.
36.nuance: The conditions rise in pressure (இடரெனினும், படைவரினும்): the rule holds in distress and even under attack. Line 2 is obscure: மாசுணி கீழ் is read as a soiled lower garment.

norm.note: a rule of the period on fire, spitting and the handling of clothes

37.reading: The verse says that those who know aram do not even look at five things: another's wife, toddy, theft, gambling and killing, because besides being scorned as worthless they are driven down the road to hell.
37.nuance: The bar is on looking (நோக்கார்), not only on doing. The verse gives two sanctions, one in this world (scorn) and one after it (hell). An ethics verse inside the ritual book, it needs no norm.

items.claim: another man's wife is not looked at by those who know aram
toddy is not looked at by them
theft is not looked at by them
gambling is not looked at by them
killing is not looked at by them

38.reading: The verse says that those of clear insight do not even think of four things: lying, slander, seizing what is another's and envy, because thinking of them brings suspicion, drives one into hard hell, and makes even the deity destroy one.
38.nuance: The bar moves inward from the eye in 37 to the mind (சிந்தியார்). ஐயம் புகுவித்து is read as bringing one under suspicion; it might instead mean bringing doubt into one's own mind.

items.claim: lying is not thought of by those of clear insight
slander is not thought of by them
seizing another's goods is not thought of by them
envy is not thought of by them

39.reading: The verse says that the worthy do not set a pot on the fire for themselves alone, do not take food for their own sake, do not let the kitchen be touched by எச்சில், and eat only after seeing the house offering fed.
39.nuance: Sharing and purity are joined in one rule of the hearth: cooking for oneself and defiling the kitchen are barred together, and the offering (மனைப்பலி) must be fed before the household eats.

norm.note: a rule of the period on the kitchen and the household offering before the meal

40.reading: The verse says that where elders and young kin are eating, one does not sit above them and does not wound them inwardly, even if they have done one great harm.
40.nuance: Forbearance is placed at the table and limited to kin: the meal is a time when even a grave wrong is not to be answered. உள்ளழிவு is read as hurt to the feelings.

norm.note: a rule of precedence of the period when kin are eating

links.note: Kural 43 names five the householder must tend (ancestors, gods, guests, kin, self); Acharakkovai 21 names five who must be fed before the householder eats: guests, elders, the cow, caged creatures and children.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kural's general duty to five becomes a sequence at the meal, and the circle of dependants widens from kin and gods to animals and captives, while the self drops off the list.
links.list_adds: It turns a list of duties into an order of serving, and it puts the cow and the caged creature beside guests and elders as claimants on the same meal.

links.note: Naladiyar 94 asks for daily giving before eating, even a grain's worth, to anyone; Acharakkovai 21 names who must be served before the meal.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar makes giving before eating a matter of amount, however small, while the Acharakkovai makes it a matter of persons, so the two together fix both how little suffices and to whom it is owed.
links.list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's unnamed recipient with five named dependants of the house, human and animal.

links.note: Verse 21 names five to be fed before one eats; verse 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
links.teaches: Together they show that the code puts others before the eater at both ends of the meal: in cooking (39) and in serving (21), with the house offering added to the living claimants.

links.note: Verse 22 bars laying the bed along the roof-ridge; verse 30 bars the head to the north and the corners when lying down.
links.teaches: Read together, the bed is governed by two separate direction rules, one tied to the house's ridge and one to the compass, so the code fixes sleep by both the building and the quarters.

links.note: Kural 946 grounds not eating to excess in health and joy; Acharakkovai 23 bars excess even when the food is choice, among rules of posture and place.
links.teaches: The same restraint has two grounds: in the Kural it pays in pleasure and freedom from disease, in the Acharakkovai it is decorum, binding even when the food tempts, so moderation is both prudence and conduct.
links.list_adds: It sets overeating beside eating lying down, standing, in the open and on the bed, so excess becomes a breach of form like a wrong posture rather than a danger to health.

links.note: Verse 20 sets the eater's direction, posture and silence; verse 25 sets the order of the food by taste, sweet first and bitter last.
links.teaches: Verse 20 governs only the eater's body, and verse 25 completes the meal code by governing the food's sequence, so the rule reaches what is eaten as well as how.

links.note: Acharakkovai 31 forbids passing between brahmins (பார்ப்பார்) as between gods; Tirumanthiram 231 denies the name of brahmin to those who lack truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion.
links.teaches: The Acharakkovai's deference attaches to the birth-name with no condition, while the Tirumanthiram makes the name itself depend on inner qualities, so the second would void the rule's deference for a brahmin who lacks them.

links.note: Verse 32 lists ten places barred for spitting and excretion; verse 34 says where these are allowed, a screened or secluded place, and sets the stake at refusing even Indra's throne.
links.teaches: Together they give the rule's two sides, the barred places and the permitted one, and verse 34 adds that the screening is also an act of mind, so the code of bodily acts reaches into intention.

links.note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, toddy and dice as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Acharakkovai 37 bars even looking at another's wife, toddy, theft, gambling and killing.
links.teaches: The Kural's sanction is loss of fortune in this life, while the Acharakkovai adds public scorn and hell, and it shifts the sexual fault from the courtesan to another's wife, so the same cluster of vices is judged on different grounds.
links.list_adds: It adds theft and killing to the Kural's three, so pleasures and crimes stand in one list, and it bars them at the level of sight.

links.note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the gambling ground; Acharakkovai 37 bars looking at five things, among them killing and gambling.
links.teaches: Both works bar the eye, but the Elathi bars the places where killing and gambling happen while the Acharakkovai bars the acts themselves and gives hell as the reason, so the ban on looking is applied once to sites and once to deeds.

links.note: Verse 37 bars looking at five wrongs; verse 38 bars even thinking of four more.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses move the ban inward from the eye to the mind, and both name hell as the end, so the code treats sight and thought as stages of the same fault.

links.note: Kural 282 says that even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; Acharakkovai 38 bars thinking of seizing, along with lying, slander and envy.
links.teaches: The Kural's thought-crime is confined to theft, and the Acharakkovai extends the same inward standard to speech faults and envy and names its sanctions, suspicion, hell and the deity's wrath.
links.list_adds: It groups seizing with lying, slander and envy, so faults of hand, tongue and heart are all forbidden at the stage of thought.

links.note: Kural 229 calls eating alone from one's hoard worse than begging; Acharakkovai 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
links.teaches: The Kural condemns eating alone by its bitterness, while the Acharakkovai moves the bar back to the hearth, so the fault begins when the pot is set on the fire for oneself.
links.list_adds: It sets the bar on solitary cooking beside a purity rule for the kitchen and an offering rule, so sharing becomes part of the ritual order of the house.

links.note: Kural 987 asks one to do good even to those who have done harm; Acharakkovai 40 asks only that one not wound elders and young kin at their meal, even if they have done great harm.
links.teaches: Set beside the Kural's universal demand, the Acharakkovai's rule is narrower in scope (kin, at the meal) and lower in demand (not harming rather than doing good), so the code fixes a minimum where the Kural sets an ideal.
links.list_adds: It joins forbearance to a seating rule (not sitting above them), so restraint toward kin is part of the precedence of the table.

source_issues: Verse 38 line 1 had ௌ written as ெ + ள (repaired to வௌவல்), and the comparison site's text lacks line 1.
Verse 22 is obscure throughout; the sense of முகட்டு வழி decides the reading.
Verse 32 counts ten (ஈரைந்தின்); the ten are reached by taking புற் and பைங்கூழ் as two and தேவ குலம் and நிழல் as two; வெண்பலி is doubtful.
